summary: This informational memo introduces TESLA, a method that lets every receiver of a multicast or broadcast stream check the integrity and source of each packet. It needs no trust between receivers and uses little work per packet.

plainLanguage.summary: TESLA lets multicast receivers check whether packets came from the sender without sharing a key that would let receivers forge packets. It delays authentication until the sender reveals the key, so receivers need loosely synchronized clocks and must buffer packets.

questions: how does tesla authenticate multicast packets
what is key disclosure delay in tesla
why cant mac be used for multicast
subtitle: A multicast authentication method that delays disclosure of packet keys so receivers can verify each message.

tldr.problem: A shared message-authentication key lets any receiver forge messages for other receivers, while signing every multicast packet has high computation and bandwidth costs.
tldr.mechanism: TESLA uses a one-way key chain and delayed key disclosure. Receivers use synchronized time to decide whether a packet arrived while its authentication key was still secret, then verify the buffered packet when the key is disclosed.
tldr.outcome: TESLA provides loss-tolerant packet authentication with low per-packet cost, but authentication is delayed and the scheme does not provide non-repudiation.

facts.label: Disclosure delay
facts.value: d must be at least 2; d=1 does not work

facts.label: Authentication delay
facts.value: In practice, on the order of one round-trip time

facts.label: Relative efficiency stated
facts.value: Symmetric cryptography is generally 3 to 5 orders of magnitude more efficient than asymmetric cryptography

today: RFC 4082 is an Informational RFC published in June 2005, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It introduces TESLA to assist the development of secure specifications based on the method.

sections.title: Why Multicast Authentication Is Different
sections.content:
In multicast, a single packet can reach many receivers, including a malicious one. A shared message authentication code (MAC) key is not enough to authenticate the sender, because every receiver that can verify the MAC could also create one.

Digital signatures provide a way for receivers to verify messages without being able to sign new ones, but signing each packet has high computation and bandwidth costs. TESLA uses symmetric cryptography and delayed key disclosure to provide the needed asymmetry. It requires loose time synchronization, and it does not provide non-repudiation to third parties.
sections.plainLanguage: A shared MAC key cannot prove that a multicast packet came from the sender, because every receiver also knows the key. TESLA uses time-delayed key disclosure to let receivers verify messages without signing every packet.

sections.title: One-Way Key Chain and Disclosure Schedule
sections.content:
The sender assigns a key from a one-way chain to each time interval. It uses the key for that interval to calculate a MAC for each packet, then discloses the key after a configured delay. Receivers know the schedule and use their time bound to check whether the key was still secret when a packet arrived.

The sender chooses the interval length T_int, a chain length N, and a disclosure delay d. The chain length limits how long the sender can transmit before creating another chain. A separate one-way function derives the MAC key from the chain key so that the same key is not reused for different cryptographic operations.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender uses a different chain key for each time interval and reveals each key later. A receiver accepts a packet for delayed checking only if it arrived before its key could have been disclosed.

sections.title: Receiver Setup and Packet Verification
sections.content:
Before authenticating packets, a receiver needs an upper bound on how far its clock lags the sender's, an authenticated key from the one-way chain, and the disclosure schedule. The receiver and sender can determine a time bound with an authenticated exchange; TESLA must be bootstrapped through a regular data-authentication system.

When a packet arrives, the receiver first checks whether it is safe under the sender's possible clock time. Safe packets are buffered. The receiver then checks that a newly disclosed key belongs to the chain and uses it to verify the MACs of earlier buffered packets. Packets with unsafe timing or an invalid key are not authenticated and should be discarded.
sections.plainLanguage: A receiver first establishes an authenticated starting key and a bound on clock difference. It buffers packets that arrived before their key was disclosed, then checks their MACs when that key becomes available.

sections.title: Choosing the Key Disclosure Delay
sections.content:
The disclosure delay affects performance, not the security guarantee. If it is too short, some packets arrive after their key is disclosed and cannot be authenticated. If it is too long, receivers wait longer before authentication.

For direct synchronization, the RFC recommends choosing d = ceil(2m / T_int) + 1, where 2m is a reasonable upper bound on the round-trip time, including congestion and host-stack buffering. A delay of one interval does not work. If actual network delay is longer than expected, authentic packets may be rejected, but an inauthentic packet will not be accepted as authentic.
sections.plainLanguage: The delay must allow packets to arrive before their keys are revealed, but a longer delay makes receivers wait more. Unexpected network delay can make genuine packets unverifiable, not make fake packets pass verification.

sections.title: Denial of Service and Layer Placement
sections.content:
Delayed authentication requires buffering, so a flood of bogus packets could consume receiver resources. The RFC suggests checking session validity, rejecting replays and unusually large packets, and limiting how far a receiver follows the key chain for misordered packets. Stronger options include adding a group MAC, not reusing a MAC key, or moving buffering to the sender; each has additional costs.

TESLA can be placed at the network, transport, or application layer. Network-layer checking means upper layers receive authenticated data, while transport- or application-layer placement avoids changes to the network layer but can add buffering delay. The timing checks are a particularly delicate implementation point.
sections.plainLanguage: Because receivers hold packets before checking them, they need safeguards against floods of invalid packets. TESLA can run at different network layers, but buffering and hidden packet delays affect its performance.

data.title: Packet construction
data.code:
P_j = {M_j || i || MAC(K'_i, M_j) || K_{i-d}}
d = ceil(2m / T_int) + 1
